pezzi.6: OpenClaw, Claude Code, Codex, MCP servers, n8n, PostgreSQL, Docker: the tools I work with every day and the precise place each one takes.
pezzi.35: What I work with, and what I do with it
pezzi.36: Not a list of brands: for every tool there is the place it takes in the systems I build. The architectures are the public ones of the respective projects, not versions of my own.
pezzi.37: I use and compare every model and every agent in circulation. Something new comes out every week: the choice has to be made again, not inherited. Trademarks belong to their respective owners and are named only to say which tools I use.
pezzi.50: An agent system is made of pieces that each do one thing. When one of them has to be replaced, that piece is replaced and not the system.
pezzi.53: Open source environment for running agents connected to real tools. I use it as the base on which to build and supervise teams of agents: I give them tools, permissions and a log of what they have done.
pezzi.57: Command line agent for working on the code of a project. I use it to build and maintain the systems I deliver, and to show in training how an agent works when it has the right permissions.
pezzi.61: The protocol through which an agent sees the operations available instead of improvising them. I write the servers that expose to the model only the permitted operations: that is where the boundary runs.
pezzi.65: I use it and compare it on multi-step tasks, where what counts is how an agent holds up when it is left to work alone for many iterations.
pezzi.68: Where the work is repetitive and verifiable, a workflow costs less than an agent and it’s more predictable when it breaks. Which of the two I use depends on the case, not on what I’m used to.
pezzi.72: The permissions sit in the database: roles, views, row level rules. An agent cannot read what its role does not see, whatever it is asked to do.
pezzi.76: Every run sits in a container with its own resources and its own limits. If something goes wrong, it goes wrong inside a perimeter.
pezzi.78: When the data does not leave
pezzi.80: When the constraint is that the data must not leave the network, the model runs on the client machine. The cost is in expertise, not in usage.
pezzi.83: The order matters more than the choice of pieces. An agent gets its tools from an MCP server, its permissions from the database and the operating system, and a log that says what it did and on what evidence.
pezzi.85: An MCP server in front of every operation
pezzi.87: Roles in the database, not sentences in the prompt
pezzi.91: Every action traces back to a read
pezzi.93: The tools change every month. The order they sit in does not.
pezzi.95: None of these tools is mine, and I have no partnership with the people who make them: I use them, compare them and replace them when they stop being the right choice. If a project listed here changes its architecture, the way I use it changes too.
